messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 36
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Detective
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 74

He remembers the smell of turmeric and cumin, the clatter of steel utensils in the kitchen sink. That was always the sound before. His mother would be washing dishes, her back to him, her bangles ringing like a warning bell. Then his father’s footsteps. Then the leather belt. He was seven, or maybe eight—he’s not sure anymore. What he remembers clearly is the precision: the way his father would fold the belt double, the single strike across his thighs, the instruction to stand still and not cry. He learned not to cry. He learned to count the seconds until it was over.

At thirty-six, Detective Rohan still counts. Not seconds, but steps. Exits. The number of hands visible in a room. He sits across from a witness in the interview room, and while she talks about a stolen car, he notes the flicker of the overhead light, the angle of the door, the weight of his service weapon against his hip. He tells himself this is situational awareness. It’s what makes him good at his job. But he knows, in the quiet moments, that it never stops. Even at home, even when his wife Priya turns over in bed and her hand brushes his arm, he flinches before he can stop himself. She doesn’t say anything anymore. She just moves her hand away.

The worst nights are when the call comes in. A domestic disturbance. A father who lost his temper. Rohan drives to the address, and his hands vibrate on the steering wheel. He stands at the door, hears the muffled shouting, and for a second he is seven years old again, listening to the sound of his own heart in the hallway. He knocks. He takes the report. He watches the mother lie, watches the child stare at the floor. He writes it all down in his notebook, neat block letters, and later he drives home and sits in the dark garage for twenty minutes before he can go inside.

Priya wants children. She has wanted them for three years. Every time she brings it up, Rohan feels the words clot in his throat. He says he’s not ready. He says the job is too demanding. The real reason sits at the bottom of him like a stone: he is terrified of becoming his father. He rehearses every interaction with a child in his head before it happens—a neighbor’s toddler, a victim’s son—and he finds himself holding his breath, monitoring his own hands, afraid that some invisible line will be crossed. He does not talk about this. He cannot.

At the station, his colleagues call him “the ice man.” Calm under pressure. Never rattled. They don’t see the way he checks the rearview mirror three times before turning onto his street. They don’t know that he keeps a packed bag in the trunk of his car, just in case. He has never told anyone about the belt, about the counting, about the way his body still braces for impact when his boss calls him into the office. He has never told Priya why he flinches. He has never told her that sometimes, when she raises her voice in an argument, his vision goes grey and he stops hearing her words.

He wakes at 3:47 every morning. The same time. He lies in the dark and feels the cold sweat on his chest and thinks about the father he arrested last week, the one who hit his son with a wooden spoon. Rohan processed the booking paperwork without a word. He drove home. He sat in the garage. He did not sleep.

He tells himself it was a long time ago. He tells himself he is not that child anymore. But at night, lying next to his wife in their quiet house, he is still seven years old, still waiting for the belt to fall.
